newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek PM holds meetings over talks with Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Greek PM holds meetings over talks with Turkey.

text.p: Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis held urgent meetings with his senior ministers on Thursday to discuss a European Union initiative for the start of a dialogue with rival Turkey, government officials said.

Simitis held separate meetings with Foreign Minister Theodore Pangalos, Defence Minister Akis Tsohatzopoulos and Alternate Foreign Minister George Papandreou. A roundtable meeting was scheduled for Thursday evening.

Government officials said Athens and Ankara were close in agreeing to the setting up of two committees of experts -- one from each side -- to discuss ways to tackle differences, including territorial feuds in the Aegean Sea.

"The fact that there can be a discussion is positive on its own," government spokesmnan Dimitris Reppas told reporters. "If we have an agreement the committees will seek a procedure with which matters can be addressed."
It is the first time the two NATO allies have considered talking since January last year when they came close to war over rights of two uninhabited islets in the eastern Aegean Sea.
The sudden rapprochement was scored on Wednesday in a Malta meeting between Papandreou and his Turkish counterpart Onur Oymen where the EU initiative was put on the table.
They were both attending a two-day conference of European and Mediterranean foreign ministers.

"Progress (has been made) in discussions between Greece and Turkey in the problems they have," said Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency. "A breakthrough took place today and we shall see the results in the future."
Reppas said the committees will "express the positions of each government and explore the positions of the other side".
Greece and Turkey have long been at odds over territorial differences in the Aegean Sea, a Moslem minority in northern Greece and the divided island of Cyprus.

Pangalos said earlier this month a dialogue with Turkey would only be possible if Ankara denounced war threats towards Greece, talks began on the accession of Cyprus to the EU and territorial differences were resolved through international courts.
But government officials said that although Greece stood firm on the three conditions they were not a prerequisite for setting up the meeting of the two committees.
Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller has said Turkey would go to war if Greece extends its territorial waters from six to 12 miles in the Aegean Sea separating the two countries.

Pangalos has said scheduled talks for Cyprus to become an EU member should begin before the end of the Dutch presidency in June and that the internationally recognised Greek-Cypriot government in Nicosia should represent the island in the talks.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkish troops invaded and occupied its northern third after a coup attempt in Nicosia engineered by a military junta then ruling Greece.

A number of Greece's EU partners, including Germany and Britain, said in February Cypriot accession would be politically and almost physically impossible without at least some progress between the island's Greek and Turkish communities.
